Author: @Josh.Davidson
Content: EE Student here: The yellowish substance you see surrounding the die is the underfill. It provides structural support to the C4 bump array bonding the die to the green substrate interposer. It is critical that the underfill chemistry is compatible with the bump material (various lead free, high-lead, eutectic, etc), and compatible with the thermal stress the connection will go under. It's just a different type of underfill vs what you're used to seeing, with a different chemistry. But as long as it meets all the required constraints then it will be fine. Fun fact, failure to choose a proper underfill type is what caused the Xbox 360 RROD, PS3 YLOD, and notebook GPU failures a nearly 15 years ago.

Author: @nathangamble125
Content:
I definitely wouldn't say that Intel fixed their problems.
This is still a GPU die almost as large as AD104 (full die = RTX 4070 Ti), on a similar manufacturing process (both are built on variants of TSMC N5), which is less than 2/3 as fast, almost 2 years later. The "Battlemage" architecture is objectively bad.
Intel deserves praise from gamers, for giving us good performance for a good price, but it's likely that Intel is losing money or barely breaking even on every B580 they sell. Intel could benefit in the long run from taking GPU market share and having a solid platform for driver development, but this will only be useful if Intel can make their next-gen "Celestial" GPUs significantly cheaper to manufacture, while still having competitive performance, so they can actually profit from it. If Celestial isn't successful, Intel will have just wasted money by pricing Battlemage so low.

Content: That die is huge!  Silicon wafer size is set when a technology node (3nm for ex) is developed.  Which means fab time is set for the most part as well, because the machinery is spun up at the same time as the node.  Yield and fab width (parallel production lines) may improve over time, but die size is a major driver of cost.  This is not a cheap chip to manufacture.

Author: @marsovac
Content:
Battlemage breakdown:
$90 for GPU die (200 dies on 4nm wafer with 90% yield) +
$75 for 12GB GDDR6 19Gbps +
$30 for a sub 200W GPU board +
$25 for cooling, backplate and assembly
shipping a 20ft container with 4000 boxes makes the shipping cost negligible
_________
$230 Total cost, $250 retail price
~10% possible profit, 20$ per unit
_________
Let's say Intel keeps all the profit, instead of sharing with the parters, mega generous here.
Nvidia ships about 9M desktop cards in a quarter (36/y) and has 90% marketshare.
So about 40M desktop cards are sold yearly.

Taking 10% would sell 4M copies. But let's be realistic, Alchemist got to 0.8%,
Battlemage won't get to 10% since they don't have the manufacturing capacity to keep the price.
Let's go with a generous 5%. This is also generous because Intel doesn't sell professional gpus,
and the numbers above include those.

So Intel breaks even in under a year if it takes 5% of the market. 
Considering GPUs don't sell much after two years and drop in price,
one year of RoI, one year of sales for profit would generate 40M.

Now this 40M is what you can invest into your next GPU development.
And now follows how much has Nvidia invested into resource and development in 2023.

8.7 BILLION!!!, I assume more than 5B of that in GPUs or 125 times more.

If miracoulously Intel took half the marketshare Nvidia would still be investing 6 times more.
In that scenario AMD would also be investing more than double of what Intel could. 
Even if Intel were the top dog they would start lagging behind more and more.
You need to invest billions.

That's a David vs Goliath if I've seen one.
IMHO Arc is not an achievable concept in the long run.
A mere miracle would not be enough, it needs the direct intervention of god in multiple affairs.
A failing Intel cannot finance this race.

I cross the fingers for Celestial, but have no hopes.
The only divine intervention I could foresee is that Intel fixes its fabs, and can produce GPUs in house, but that alone is not enough.

Author: @DannyWilliamH
Content:
Heat causes the discoloration of the epoxy/bonding. 

In a lot of older devices the color alone is an indicator of the health of the die itself.

If I'm being honest, that's not as true today from my experience. The last major tech device I stil repair a lot of where the color of the epoxy gave an indication of health was The Switch.

So I won't say that the discoloration  here is or isn't a big deal but it's, at worst, bad and at best nothing. It's definitely not a good thing.
